title: The ten-day retreat, going home
hookLine: the hardest part: carrying the calm into ordinary life

cards: The envelope comes back. Inside, the phone, and when it wakes it starts buzzing and doesn't stop: messages, alerts, a calendar full of next week. The drive home has traffic.

The grocery store on the way is louder than you remember, and brighter. Someone cuts in line, and something old and hot rises in the chest, right on schedule. On the last morning, the calm felt solid enough to stand on.
By dinner, it's thinner. Teachers of these retreats often say this is where the real work starts.

teach.b: First, the thinning. A retreat's calm was made in special conditions: silence, bells, no choices. Out here those conditions are gone, and the calm fades.
Teachers say that's normal, and that the calm was never really the point. The point was learning to see the mind, and that can come home. Second, an old Zen picture of it.
The ox-herding pictures are a series of Zen images.
A herder searches for a lost ox, a picture of the mind, finds its tracks, catches it, tames it, rides it home. Then herder and ox both vanish into an empty circle. But the series doesn't stop there.
In its last picture, the herder walks into the town marketplace, barefoot, belly round, hands open, mixing with ordinary people.
The verse with it says he has no need of special powers; the withered trees bloom wherever he goes. The path doesn't end on the mountain. It ends in the market.
Third, one habit. Teachers on retreat courses encourage some practice at home: a sit in the morning or evening, a pause before eating, a day of silence now and then.
Some students go home vowing to keep everything and keep nothing.
One habit, kept, carries further. Fourth, the test.

teach.h: THE PRACTICE LIVES AT HOME NOW.
teach.b: The person who cuts in line, the coworker, the family at the dinner table: that's where the practice now lives.
The retreat wasn't an escape from ordinary life. It was training for it.

how: After a meditation retreat, Buddhist teachers commonly encourage students to keep a regular practice at home, such as a daily sit, and to bring the retreat's attention into work, family and ordinary errands.

o: a break from life that has nothing to do with home
a retreat that leaves you calm for good afterward
a silent retreat whose real work starts on the drive home

p: small enough for a bad day

s: if the calm fades after a retreat, the retreat failed
teachers say fading is normal; the calm was made in special conditions.
the ox-herding pictures end on a mountaintop
the last picture shows the herder walking into the marketplace, hands open.
retreats are meant as training for ordinary life
the practice now lives at home, in traffic and at the dinner table.

games.q: you're home from a retreat, full of resolve. what do you take on?
o: keep every part of the retreat schedule at once.
keep one small habit you can do even on a bad day.
wait until the next retreat to practice again.
games.why: teachers encourage some practice at home. one habit, kept, carries further than many dropped.

practice: Sit and breathe, then choose one retreat habit small enough to do even on a bad day: a few breaths before you look at your phone, a pause before meals, a short sit at night.
See yourself doing it tomorrow, in your actual kitchen, then let the choice rest and come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: The ten-day retreat. Its last lesson comes after it ends: carrying what was learned in silence back into traffic, kitchens and crowded rooms. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali bhavana: cultivation, bringing into being; the word often used for meditation as an ongoing practice.

carryVoice: Your line: carry it home. The retreat ends the moment you drive away, and then, slowly, it begins again. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: The ox-herding pictures (Kuoan Shiyuan's verses), final picture
